A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SLM-MUX. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and newly added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments, model-selection and compute-scaling results in Section 4, and debate-failure analysis in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds prompt-sensitivity, design-validation, HumanEval, frontier-model, and specialist-model experiments in Appendices C–E.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the model-selection procedure are retained. Appendix E.1 adds a code-generation adaptation that replaces exact-answer frequency with CodeT5+ embeddings, pairwise cosine similarities, and a coherent-cluster fraction for estimating confidence. This changes one inference component for the extension.

E1.justification: v2 adds HumanEval code generation to the retained MATH, GPQA, and GSM8K evaluations. This substantially extends task coverage from discrete-answer reasoning to open-ended executable-code generation; the additional frontier and specialist model configurations largely reuse these tasks.

E2.justification: The original orchestration comparators remain, including Single-Best-SC, which was already reported in v1 Table 1. v2 adds evaluated prompt-optimized MoA variants in Appendix C.2/Table 9 and constituent-model comparisons involving Gemini-2.5-Flash and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B in Appendix E.

E3.justification: New protocols include HumanEval Pass@1 evaluation with five samples per model at temperature 0.3, varying search-set sizes, random model subsets, and test-set scaling across K=1–5. Appendix C.2 also evaluates ten generated MoA prompts and six rounds of optimization directly on the test set. These are added evaluation designs; the original experiments' stated sampling settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether the baseline gap depends on prompts, whether consistency predicts correctness, whether model rankings withstand smaller search sets, whether gains persist without optimized model selection, and whether scaling trends transfer to test data. These appear in Appendices C.2 and D.1–D.4. The original groupthink analysis is retained in C.1.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3/Table 7 newly reports Bernoulli standard errors for Figure 5, although it calls them standard deviations, and Figure 15 reports Pearson correlations. Existing three-run descriptions and uncertainty reporting in Tables 1–4 remain; the PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include HumanEval Pass@1 of 0.506 and 0.939 (Table 14), frontier-model GPQA accuracy of 60.1% (Table 15), and random-selection and test-set scaling outcomes (Tables 10–12). Original Tables 1–4 retain their values. Figure 5 changes MoA's MATH accuracy from 51.4% to 46.2%, creating an unresolved disagreement with the retained 51.4% in Table 1.

T1.justification: Section 5 adds answer-distribution and positive model-margin assumptions, then derives a Hoeffding/union-bound guarantee for selecting the strongest model, with error decreasing exponentially in sample count. v1 had no corresponding selection guarantee. Its binomial comparison of self-consistency, SLM-MUX, and Agent Forest is retained in v2 Appendix D.2.

C1.justification: The central orchestration, model-selection, and two-SLM-versus-Qwen-72B claims remain. The abstract adds an explicit generalization claim covering open-ended HumanEval generation, frontier LLMs, and domain-specific fine-tuned models.

C2.justification: v2 adds an upper/lower-bound rationale for the search objective, interprets prompt-optimization results as evidence of inherent aggregation limitations, argues that search improves an already robust architecture, and attributes limited frontier gains to overlapping correct predictions. These substantially expand the scientific interpretation. The existing limitations concerning static model sets and confidently incorrect outputs remain.

D1.justification: Appendix E specifies the CodeT5+ embedding checkpoint, similarity-matrix computation, alternative Qwen2.5-7B judge, model pairings, and sampling settings for the extensions. Figure 5 newly discloses temperature-zero decoding for discussion baselines. These additions improve documentation without establishing that previously reported experiments changed settings.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chen et al. (2021), Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code, and Fu et al. (2025), Cache-to-Cache. The broader positioning relative to discussion-based orchestration, model selection, and test-time scaling remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. Local rewrites clarify self-consistency and search, while the appendix is regrouped: original single-model results move from D to B.2, and the original mathematical discussion moves from Section 5 to D.2. Author notes and several explanations are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 15–17 for consistency, ranking stability, and test-set scaling, plus Tables 7 and 9–16 for uncertainty, sensitivity, selection, and generalization results. Existing appendix tables are relocated and several captions expanded. This substantially expands the evidentiary displays while retaining most original figures and tables.

improvement.justification: The new prompt controls, random-selection analyses, direct consistency validation, and held-out scaling results address important untested assumptions in v1. HumanEval and additional model-class experiments further strengthen empirical support for applicability. These are substantial evidential gains, despite the new MoA discrepancy between Figure 5 and Table 1 and incomplete specification of the semantic-clustering procedure.
